archetype.name: Super Bowl Contender (offense-led)
archetype.definition: San Francisco has the league's most efficient offense and its best point differential through four weeks, with a middling defense that has kept scores down by allowing almost no big plays and holding up in the red zone.

report.headline: Best offense in football so far, with a defense living on red-zone stops
report.take:
Four games in, San Francisco is the best team in the league by the numbers that matter most. They lead in net EPA, offensive EPA, passing EPA and offensive success rate, and their point differential of 14.5 per game is also first. Their 0.267 net EPA is higher than any season in their recent history, including the 2023 team that led the league at 0.234. This is not a repeat of 2025, when a 12-5 record sat on a 15th-ranked net EPA, 2.62 wins over expected and an 0.833 one-score win rate. The 2026 team is winning by margin. Only one of the four wins, the 36-30 shootout with Arizona, was close.

The engine is protection. Brock Purdy has not been sacked once in four games. He has been pressured on under 10% of dropbacks and hit 11 times, all first in the league. With that much time he spreads the ball across four targets: Mike Evans 24, Christian McCaffrey 22, George Kittle 22, Deebo Samuel 17. That is the classic Shanahan passing game at full strength. The same line gives runners 3.39 yards before contact, second in the league, and stuffs only 15.5% of runs. Still, rushing EPA was negative in three of four games. The run game moves the chains and sets up play-action more than it produces value on its own.

The schedule hides some things. The two huge passing games, 23.3 and 22.9 EPA, came against Miami and Arizona, whose defenses rank 28th and 27th. Against the Rams' fourth-ranked defense in Week 1 the passing game produced 4.8 EPA, and the 27-7 win leaned on 174 rushing yards. The defense ranks third in points allowed but only 14th in EPA and 19th in success rate allowed. It sits 24th on third down and 25th in sacks. It keeps scores low by allowing almost nothing explosive (first against the run, second against the pass) and by forcing field goals: 45.5% red-zone TD rate, fifth best. Red-zone rates are noisy over four games. A defense that gives up 44% of third downs and has six sacks is closer to average than its scoring line suggests.

The injury news hits that soft spot directly. Nick Bosa (calf) is out, DT James Thompson is out, and starting safety Marques Sigle (88% of snaps) has a high-ankle sprain expected to cost multiple weeks. Fullback Kyle Juszczyk is also likely gone for several weeks. The back half of the schedule brings top-10 defenses in Minnesota, Las Vegas, Seattle twice, the Rams, Atlanta and Kansas City. Expect the offense to come back to earth somewhat while the defense gets thinner. It is still a team built to win the division, but the 30-points-a-game pace will fade.

strengths.title: Spotless pass protection
strengths.body: Zero sacks, a league-best 9.8% pressure rate and the fewest QB hits allowed, while Purdy holds the ball a fairly normal 2.96 seconds. That combination points to a well-coordinated line and scheme, not just quick throws. A zero sack rate can't last, but protection this good through four games is likely to stay top-five.

strengths.title: Most efficient passing game in football
strengths.body: Passing EPA of 0.539 per play and a 54.1% success rate both lead the league, with the work spread across Evans, McCaffrey, Kittle and Samuel. The defenses faced inflate it, since two of the four games came against bottom-six units. A deep, balanced set of targets is the sustainable part. Expect it to drift toward very good rather than historic.

strengths.title: Defense allows nothing explosive
strengths.body: San Francisco ranks first in explosive rush rate allowed, second in explosive pass rate and fourth in deep-pass EPA allowed. Opponents have to drive the length of the field, and the red zone has been the payoff. That approach is real, but it depends on safety play, and Sigle's ankle injury tests it.

concerns.title: No pass rush, and Bosa is out
concerns.body: Six sacks (25th) and a 13% QB hit rate (27th) mean quarterbacks have been comfortable against this front. Bosa has played only two games and is out again, and DT Thompson is out too. This is a real flaw in the roster as it stands, not a side effect of the scheme, and it explains the 23rd-ranked EPA allowed on short throws.

concerns.title: Points allowed flatter the defense
concerns.body: Third in points allowed but 14th in EPA allowed, 19th in success rate and 24th on third down. The gap is mostly a strong red-zone TD rate and a lack of big plays allowed. Red-zone defense regresses hard over small samples, so expect points allowed to rise toward the high teens or low 20s.

concerns.title: Run game is volume, not value
concerns.body: The line creates room, but rushing EPA is still negative per play and was below zero in three of four games. The 174-yard opener against the Rams carried most of the season's rushing value. Juszczyk's knee sprain removes a key blocker. Against good run defenses the offense will rest almost entirely on Purdy.

trend.note: The results have been uniformly good (4-0, 3-1 ATS), but the size of the passing output has followed opponent quality: 4.8 and 8.5 pass EPA against the Rams and Broncos, more than 22 against Miami and Arizona. The defense's worst day, 30 points allowed, came against Arizona in Week 3, and it allowed 14 to Denver in Week 4.

nextGame.headline: Clean-pocket Purdy meets Seattle's elite defense and soft underneath zone
nextGame.body:
This is the toughest defense San Francisco has seen. Seattle ranks third in EPA allowed and second in success rate allowed, and leads the league in yards allowed per game. Its rush defense ranks fourth and its deep defense second, so the explosive plays and early-down runs that fueled the Rams win will be harder to find. The opening is underneath: Seattle ranks 28th in short-pass EPA allowed, which suits McCaffrey and Kittle on the short throws Shanahan builds on. Seattle also converts only 66.7% of red-zone trips into touchdowns allowed... rather, it allows touchdowns on 66.7% of opponent red-zone trips (22nd), so drives that get there should finish. On the other side, Seattle's offense is limited. Drew Lock has started three straight since Week 1, the run game ranks 26th in EPA, and Seattle still runs more than expected (PROE -5.1).

Availability favors Seattle on defense. San Francisco plays without Bosa and Thompson, likely without safety Sigle and fullback Juszczyk, and with Christian Kirk still on IR. Seattle expects DT Leonard Williams to play despite his ankle. Its backfield, however, is gutted: Jadarian Price is on IR and Zach Charbonnet won't come off PUP. That leaves a run game already 27th in stuff rate even thinner, which reduces how much San Francisco's weakened front gets exposed on the ground.

keyMatchups.title: 49ers protection vs Seattle's pass rush
keyMatchups.body: San Francisco's league-best protection meets a Seattle defense fourth in QB hit rate with 11 sacks. If Purdy stays clean, the underneath game should work. If Seattle wins up front, it is the first real test this line has faced.

keyMatchups.title: Short passing vs Seattle's weak spot
keyMatchups.body: Seattle shuts down deep throws but ranks 28th against short passes. San Francisco's targets are spread among a running back, a tight end and two receivers who win after the catch. Expect a high-completion, chain-moving plan rather than shots downfield.

keyMatchups.title: Special teams and penalties
keyMatchups.body: Seattle's special teams are fifth in EPA, San Francisco's 21st, which is a hidden-yardage edge for the home side. San Francisco gives some of that back on discipline, at 4.3 penalties per game against Seattle's 8.8.

nextGame.watch: Whether Seattle's pass rush can finally put Purdy on the ground. The first sack San Francisco allows this season would be the clearest sign the offense's edge is shrinking.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is genuinely elite. The protection, the spread of targets and the efficient passing are sustainable, but the remaining schedule features six top-10 defenses, so 30 points a game should settle into the mid-20s. The defense is the bigger regression risk. Its points-allowed rank rests on red-zone stops and no big plays, with no pass rush behind it, and losing Bosa, Thompson and Sigle for stretches makes the short-pass and third-down issues worse.

The overall shape is still a division winner. A 4-0 start built on margin, a one-game lead over Seattle with a home rematch in Week 12, and only Kansas City clearly matching them on both sides of the ball make 11-13 wins the reasonable range. The playoff ceiling depends on Bosa's return and on whether the pass rush can produce more than 1.5 sacks a game.
swingFactors: Bosa's return and health of the pass rush
Secondary depth while Sigle is out
Protection holding up against six top-10 defenses

bets.reason: San Francisco's net EPA of 0.267 is more than double Seattle's 0.122, yet the market prices this as a road field goal. Seattle's offense ranks 26th in rushing EPA, is down its top two backs and has had Lock under center for three weeks, which limits its ability to take advantage of San Francisco's injuries. Kept to a lean because the 49ers' numbers came mostly against weak defenses and Bosa and Sigle are out.

confidence.note: Four-game sample against mostly weak defenses, plus key defensive injuries.
